newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt agency probes shares-for-loans deals.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt agency probes shares-for-loans deals.

text.p: The State Anti-Monopoly Committee is looking into 10 transactions involving some of Russia's biggest financial-industrial groups, including controversial shares-for-loans deals, the committee's chairman said on Monday.
"There is an investigation into whether the deals, including shares-for-loans deals, made an impact on competition, whether they changed the environment," Leonid Bochin told a news conference.
Financial-industrial groups (FIGs), often built around a big bank, bring together industrial holdings in many sectors. Some FIGs are loose associations, others have complex equity cross-holdings.
The committee said in a statement there was a tendency among commercial structures to conceal property and management links.

It said the issue concerned informal FIGs built on a partnership basis and listed the Alfa group, led by Alfa-Bank, Menatep Group, led by Bank Menatep and the Rossiisky Kredit group, led by Bank Rossiisky Kredit, and the Maxim group.
Rossiisky Kredit said the committee had contacted it earlier this year but had no claims against it.

"Currently, the anti-monopoly committee is not looking into the legality of any deals made by Rossiisky Kredit or any of its clients or partners with respect to acquisitions of shares," Rossiisky Kredit vice-president Vyacheslav Korunov told Reuters.
Alfa-Bank and Bank Menatep said they would comment on Tuesday.
Bochin said the investigations dealt with the oil, mining, food-processing, trade and television sectors but declined to give any more details before the investigation was complete.
The committee said in a statement that if it found any threat to competition, it would try to declare the deals invalid through the court.
The shares-for-loans scheme, in which state-owned stakes in top companies were tendered in exchange for loans to the government late last year, proved highly controversial.
Auction winners were often close to auction organisers and winning bids were frequently barely above the starting price.
Under the scheme, Menatep won the right to manage a 45 percent stake in NK Yukos, the country's second-biggest oil group.
Rosprom, which unites Menatep's industrial holdings, now holds 52 percent of Yukos and will auction a one-third stake in an investment tender this month.
Neither Alfa-Bank nor Rossiisky Kredit won any of the auctions, despite making bids.
